evidence: Current state-of-the-art approaches suffer from noticeable visual drift: characters lose identity and objects lose defining features with each edit.
value: Class-wide property of instruction-edit models: identity and object features erode with EACH edit, so the drift is cumulative rather than a one-off failure. This is the mechanism behind 'the character stops being the same character' in iterative workflows.

evidence: Our evaluation reveals that even state-of-the-art commercial models such as GPT Image 1 ( OpenAI, 2025 ) and Seedream 3.0 ( Gao et al., 2025 ) struggle when faced with tasks requiring multi-line text rendering, non-alphabetic languages rendering (e.g., Chinese), localized text insertions, or seamless integration of text and visual elements.
value: Stated as still-unsolved across the field including GPT Image 1 and Seedream 3.0: multi-line text, non-alphabetic scripts, localized text insertion into a specified spot, and making text sit convincingly inside the scene.

Position remains the worst GenEval axis for every open-weight model in the table — SDXL 0.15, PixArt-alpha 0.08, FLUX.1-dev 0.22, SD3-Medium 0.33, CogView4-6B 0.48, and even the table's winner HiDream-I1 only 0.60 against 1.00 on Single Object. Compositional/spatial prompts are the class-wide failure, and headline 'overall' scores of 0.66-0.83 conceal it.

evidence: However, in practice, we encountered persistent artifacts such as the loss of high-frequency details and noticeable color shifts – issues that have been increasingly documented by the community.
fix: When texture sharpness or colour accuracy matters, compare a distilled checkpoint against its full-step base before shipping.
value: Few-step distilled checkpoints (the -Turbo / -schnell / -Distil class) carry two characteristic and named artifacts from standard DMD distillation: loss of high-frequency detail (blurred textures) and colour shifts. Z-Image's Decoupled DMD was built specifically to remove them, which dates the problem to standard DMD, not to the base model.

evidence: This rigorous supervision acts as an anchor, forcing the model to discard low-quality modes ( e.g. , unstable stylization or inconsistent rendering) and align strictly with detailed textual descriptions, shifting the model from a diversity-maximizing regime to a quality-maximizing operating point.
value: Supervised fine-tuning of a modern T2I model is explicitly a trade of variety for polish — the vendor describes the SFT stage as moving the model off diversity toward a narrow high-quality sub-manifold. This is the mechanism behind 'every seed looks the same' on heavily post-trained checkpoints.

evidence: Models strong in temporal consistency often have a lower Dynamic Degree, as these two aspects are somewhat complementary (see Figure 2 and Table 1). For example, LaVie excels in Background Consistency and Temporal Flickering but has a low Dynamic Degree, probably because generating relatively static scenes can "cheat" to get high temporal consistency scores.
fix: Never read a consistency score without the model's Dynamic Degree next to it; VBench isolates Dynamic Degree as a supplementary dimension for exactly this reason.
value: VBench temporal-consistency dimensions (Subject Consistency, Background Consistency, Temporal Flickering, Motion Smoothness) trade off against Dynamic Degree: a near-static video scores high on all four. LaVie is named as the example that 'cheats' this way.

evidence: For temporal consistency dimensions Subject Consistency, Background Consistency, and Temporal Flickering, a completely static video corresponds to the 100% score.
value: A completely static video is the theoretical 100% for Subject Consistency, Background Consistency and Temporal Flickering — the ceiling of those metrics is 'nothing moved', not 'identity held under motion'.

evidence:

  "temporal flickering": {"Min": 0.6293, "Max": 1.0},

fix: Compare models within a dimension only; cross-dimension deltas in percentage points are not comparable.
value: Reported VBench percentages are min-max normalized, not raw metric values. Motion Smoothness raw range is 0.7060–0.9975; Overall Consistency raw max is 0.364; Appearance Style raw range 0.0009–0.2855. A 96% Motion Smoothness is a rescaling of a ~0.99 raw score inside a 0.29-wide band.

evidence: To disentangle the evaluation of temporal flickering from other aspects, we use static video scenes (i.e., no apparent motions) as the test cases (We use carefully designed prompts to generate static scenes for video sampling. To further ensure that the evaluation is conducted on static videos without apparent motions, we employ an optical flow estimator [93] to filter out videos and only keep the static videos).
value: Temporal Flickering is measured ONLY on deliberately static scenes — every prompt in that suite carries a prefix instructing a static scene, and non-static generations are filtered out with optical flow. Flicker under real motion is not what this number measures.

evidence: Both Subject Consistency and Background Consistency focus on temporal consistency of the "look" instead of the smoothness of "movement and motion".
value: Subject Consistency is DINO feature similarity across frames and Background Consistency is CLIP feature similarity — both measure the 'look', explicitly not whether the motion is plausible; Motion Smoothness is a separate video-frame-interpolation prior.

evidence: we uniformly sample 16 frames from each video and apply UMT [65], which achieves the state-of-the-art classification performance on the Kinetics-400 dataset among open-sourced models to classify the action. The top 5 results with logits bigger than 0.85 are preserved as ground-truth candidates, and we check whether the actions mentioned in the text prompt appear in the ground-truth candidates.
value: Human Action is a Kinetics-400 top-5 classifier check (UMT), scored as 'did the prompt's action appear in the classifier's candidates' — a closed 100-action vocabulary, 16 sampled frames. It cannot say anything about action quality, and nothing about lip or face motion.

evidence: On the other hand, for categories involving complex and intense motions like Human and Vehicle (see their Dynamic Degree in Supplementary File), performance is relatively poor across all dimensions.
value: Content category matters: for Human and Vehicle prompts — the high-motion categories — performance is relatively poor across ALL VBench dimensions, not just aesthetics.

evidence: recent state-of-the-art models, including Sora [53], Kling [69], Gen-3 [59], HunyuanVideo [72], and Veo 2 [68], have demonstrated strong performance on these metrics, and many aspects of superficial faithfulness are now approaching saturation.
fix: Use VBench-2.0's intrinsic-faithfulness dimensions (Human Identity, Human Anatomy, Motion Rationality) alongside VBench-1.0 rather than instead of it.
value: The four consistency/smoothness dimensions no longer separate current models: VBench's own authors say superficial faithfulness is saturating for Sora, Kling, Gen-3, HunyuanVideo and Veo 2. Choosing a model on those five numbers is choosing on noise.

evidence: We select the first frame of the video as the anchor by default, and all subsequent frames are compared to the first frame to calculate similarity. However, time periods where there are multiple people or no one present are not taken into consideration.
value: Human Identity in VBench-2.0 is ArcFace similarity of every frame against the FIRST frame, with multi-person and no-face intervals excluded, and identity is still counted across scene cuts. Frames where the face is absent simply do not score.

evidence: Most models perform poorly in capturing Dynamic Spatial Relationships and Dynamic Attributes. Even in relatively simple cases, where an entity's position, relationship, or attribute (e.g., color) is instructed to change, and models fail in about 80% of the time.
fix: The paper blames caption granularity; practically, do not ask for a mid-clip attribute change in one prompt — cut it into separate shots.
value: Current SOTA models fail roughly 80% of the time at simple dynamic control — changing an entity's position, relationship, or colour mid-clip (Dynamic Spatial Relationship 19–21%, Dynamic Attribute 8–24% across HunyuanVideo/CogVideoX-1.5/Sora/Kling 1.6).

evidence: A major limitation is that current foundation video generative models typically produce single-shot videos under 10 seconds in length, insufficient for conveying coherent narratives.
value: Multi-scene narrative prompts collapse: Complex Plot scores are 10.11% (HunyuanVideo), 12.42% (CogVideoX-1.5), 11.67% (Sora), 11.83% (Kling 1.6), and the stated cause is that foundation models produce single-shot clips under 10 seconds.

evidence: As a result, models that produce aesthetically pleasing and smooth outputs are frequently perceived as "better". However, this perception could be misleading.
value: VBench's own authors warn that a model reading as 'better' from smooth, pretty output is a perception bias — visual quality scores are the first impression, not the applicability verdict.

evidence: fp8 support; requires newest ComfyUI and torch >= 2.1 (decreases VRAM usage, but changes outputs)
value: Running diffusion weights in fp8 is not output-neutral: it saves VRAM but changes the generated result, so a fp8 run is not a valid reproduction of a fp16 run.

evidence: While quantization wasn't feasible for regular UNET models (conv2d), transformer/DiT models such as flux seem less affected by quantization.
value: Aggressive low-bit quantization is architecture-dependent: conv2d UNet diffusion models do not survive it, while transformer/DiT models tolerate it. Quantized-video-model advice from a DiT model does not carry to a UNet one.

evidence: Second, without length-specific fine-tuning, Chimera extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos, with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds.
fix: Length-specific fine-tuning, or a hybrid long-context backbone (KDA + interleaved MLA); otherwise budget the tail of the clip as the degraded region.
value: Zero-shot length extrapolation from 5s training clips to 30s output costs ~6.5% FID degradation concentrated in the LAST five seconds — degradation is not uniform across the clip, it accumulates toward the tail.

evidence: In particular, for 240s generation, it substantially improves overall and semantic scores while reducing quality drift from 7.84 to 1.33, demonstrating its effectiveness for stable long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion.
fix: Cache partitioned into sink/memory/recent regions with gated recall (GRAB) and statistical re-alignment of recalled memory tokens (TAME).
value: Autoregressive long-form video accumulates measurable quality drift: at 240s an unmitigated Self-Forcing baseline shows drift of 7.84 on VBench-Long, reduced to 1.33 by cache management — a ~6x effect at 4-minute scale.

evidence: However, extending these models to minute-level generation remains challenging: the limited KV-cache budget prevents the model from retaining the full history, while repeatedly conditioning on self-generated frames induces a context distribution shift that accumulates over time, leading to visual artifacts, quality degradation, and temporal drift.
value: Named root cause for minute-level AR generation: fixed KV-cache budget cannot retain full history, and conditioning on self-generated frames induces a context distribution shift that compounds over time into artifacts, quality loss and temporal drift.

evidence: Experiments on 17 representative LVG models reveal pronounced capability disparities across evaluation dimensions, with strong perceptual quality and background consistency but markedly weaker fine-grained text-video alignment and character consistency.
value: Across 17 long-video generation models, character consistency and fine-grained text-video alignment are the WEAK dimensions while perceptual quality and background consistency are strong — a good-looking long clip is not evidence of a held identity.

evidence: These findings suggest that improving prompt faithfulness and identity preservation remains a key challenge for long-form video generation.
fix: Evaluate with a dimension-split framework (LoCoT2V-Eval) that scores temporal character consistency separately rather than as one aggregate score.
value: Aggregate long-video quality scores hide the failure: perceptual/background scores stay high while identity preservation and prompt faithfulness remain the open problem.

evidence: Existing benchmarks primarily focus on 5--10 second text-conditioned generation and rarely support unified evaluation across text, image, and video conditioning modalities. Moreover, they provide limited insight into how identity consistency, narrative coherence, and audio-visual alignment degrade over extended temporal horizons.
fix: LongAV-Compass: 284 minute-long test cases across T2AV/I2AV/V2AV, >20 dimensions including cross-segment consistency, scored with DINO-v2, ArcFace, CLIP and ImageBind plus MLLM assessment and human-alignment validation, run on 11 models.
value: Existing audio-visual benchmarks are confined to 5-10 second text-conditioned generation and give little insight into how identity consistency degrades over longer horizons — short-clip scores do not transfer to minute-scale work.

evidence: The framework evaluates more than 20 fine-grained dimensions covering within-segment quality, cross-segment consistency, global narrative coherence, semantic alignment, and audio-visual synchronization.
value: Minute-scale AV evaluation separates within-segment quality from cross-segment consistency and global narrative coherence — the seam between segments is a distinct failure axis from within-shot quality.

evidence: Across workflows, DirectorBench reveals a between-unit bottleneck: transition quality averages only 0.256 and reaches 0.356 for the best workflow, while prompt-level user demand fulfillment averages 0.71.
value: In long-form multi-shot workflows the measured bottleneck is BETWEEN units, not within them: transition quality averages 0.256 (best workflow 0.356) while prompt-level demand fulfillment averages 0.71 — the seam is roughly 3x worse than the shots.

evidence: The results show that DirectorBench captures human-perceptible quality differences and reveals workflow- and profile-dependent failure modes that are hidden by aggregate scoring.
fix: Score against 40 checkpoint criteria across 5 dimensions and localize the failing checkpoint instead of reducing to one number.
value: Aggregate scoring hides workflow- and profile-dependent failure modes that 14 human annotators do perceive; checkpoint-level localization was required to surface them.

evidence: Our baseline comparisons validate the necessity of this multi-stage decomposition; specifically, we observe that removing the visual anchoring mechanism results in a catastrophic drop in character consistency scores (from 7.99 to 0.55), confirming that visual priors are essential for identity preservation.
fix: Generate a character reference image per character with a T2I model first, then use it as the anchor for each scene's video generation (multi-stage decomposition).
value: Character consistency in multi-shot AI video stories collapses without an explicit per-character visual anchor image: removing the anchoring mechanism drops the consistency score from 7.99 to 0.55 (~93% loss). Text-only character description does not hold identity across scenes.

evidence: Furthermore, we analyze cultural disparities in current models, revealing distinct biases in subject consistency and dynamic degree between Indian vs Western-themed generations.
value: Measured cultural bias in subject consistency: the same pipeline shows distinct biases in subject consistency and dynamic degree between Indian-themed and Western-themed generations — identity preservation is not uniform across subject demographics.

evidence: The widely adopted chunk-wise paradigm introduces two fundamental failures: (1) temporal-spatial misalignment between static identity references and dynamic audio streams, and (2) cascading identity drift propagated through self-generated continuity references across chunks.
fix: Temporal Reference Encoding (encode the still as a temporally replicated pseudo-video) plus Asymmetric Knowledge Distillation (teacher on ground-truth continuity refs, student on self-generated refs).
value: Chunk-wise long talking-head generation has two named failures: temporal-spatial misalignment between a static identity reference and the dynamic audio stream, and cascading identity drift propagated through self-generated continuity references across chunks. Fixing both enabled identity-consistent synthesis over 600-second videos at 66 FPS.

evidence: AKD resolves the inherent conditioning dilemma in chunk-wise training: using ground-truth references causes train-inference mismatch, while self-generated references entangle supervision with identity drift.
value: Chunk-wise training faces a stated dilemma with no free option: ground-truth continuity references cause train/inference mismatch, while self-generated references entangle the supervision signal with the drift itself.

evidence: Streaming inference exacerbates these issues, leading to pronounced multimodal degradation, such as spatial blurring, temporal drift, and lip desynchronization, which creates an unresolved efficiency-performance trade-off.
fix: Hybrid Long Tail Forcing — enforce alignment on tail frames only during long-horizon self-rollout training via a causal-bidirectional hybrid architecture.
value: Streaming/real-time inference specifically amplifies degradation into three named artifacts: spatial blurring, temporal drift, and lip desynchronization — an efficiency-vs-identity trade-off the authors call unresolved.

evidence: This reliance often leads to a failure mode we term copy-paste, where the model directly replicates the reference face rather than preserving identity across natural variations in pose, expression, or lighting.
fix: Train on a large paired dataset with multiple images per identity (MultiID-2M) using a contrastive identity loss; benchmark copy-paste artifacts separately from ID similarity.
value: "Copy-paste" is a named failure mode of identity-conditioned generation trained by reconstruction: the model replicates the reference face verbatim instead of preserving identity across pose/expression/lighting variation. High ID-similarity can therefore be a symptom, not a success.

evidence: Such over-similarity undermines controllability and limits the expressive power of generation.
fix: Report ID similarity alongside a copy-paste/variation measure; a single ID-similarity number cannot distinguish preservation from replication.
value: Identity fidelity and expressive variation trade off against each other and need separate benchmark axes — over-similarity to the reference undermines controllability even while scoring well on identity metrics.

evidence: Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current baselines struggle with continuous narrative logic or degenerate into trivial 2D sticker generators, our MuSS-augmented model achieves state-of-the-art narrative effectiveness and cross-shot identity preservation.
fix: Cross-shot matching in the training data to eradicate the copy-paste shortcut, plus an Anti-Copy-Paste Variance (ACP-Var) metric to detect it.
value: Subject-to-video multi-shot baselines either fail narrative logic or degenerate into trivial 2D sticker generators — pasting the reference subject as a flat cutout across shots rather than re-rendering it 3D-consistently.

evidence: existing methods suffer from two fundamental challenges: (1) suboptimal motion injection strategies that lead to a trade-off between identity preservation and motion consistency, manifesting as a "see-saw", and (2) an over-reliance on explicit pose priors (e.g., skeletons), which inadequately capture intricate dynamics and hinder generalization to arbitrary, non-humanoid characters.
fix: Treat motion conditioning as in-context learning — fuse reference appearance and motion cues into a unified latent, and move to direct RGB-driven animation instead of skeleton priors.
value: Character animation shows a measured "see-saw": identity preservation and motion consistency trade off under existing motion-injection strategies, and explicit pose priors (skeletons) fail to capture intricate dynamics and do not generalize to non-humanoid characters.

evidence: methods based on explicit motion representations suffer from extraction errors and identity drift; methods based on implicit motion features lose fine-grained dynamics through compression; and in-context learning approaches avoid intermediate representations but incur prohibitive computational costs.
value: Character-animation paradigms fail in three distinct ways by construction: explicit motion representations produce extraction errors and identity drift; implicit motion features lose fine-grained dynamics to compression; in-context approaches avoid both but are computationally prohibitive.

evidence: However, this common masking strategy suffers from (1) information loss in the input faces, significantly affecting the networks' ability to preserve visual quality and identity details, (2) variation between identity reference and input image degrading reconstruction performance, and (3) the identity reference negatively impacting the model, causing unintended copying of elements unaligned with the audio.
fix: Mask-free approach: landmark-based closed-mouth transform of the unmasked input, then lip adaptation from audio — needs neither masked inputs nor an identity reference image.
value: Inpainting-based talking-face generation (mask the lower half, fill from audio) degrades identity three ways: information loss in the masked input, reconstruction degradation from reference/input variation, and unintended copying of reference elements unaligned with the audio.

evidence: However, end-to-end video generators are prone to appearance drift as motion accumulates and the depicted actions change.
fix: Keyframe-anchored pipeline: condition each keyframe jointly on the reference identity AND its predecessor, decoupling time-invariant appearance from time-varying pose, then fill intermediate segments with multi-reference guidance and identity-driven noise searching.
value: Identity/appearance drift is driven by accumulated motion and action change, not elapsed frames alone — a scripted multi-action clip drifts faster than a static-subject clip of the same length.

evidence: Recent commercial video generation models have achieved strong visual quality and motion realism, but they still suffer from identity drift, incomplete instruction following, and missing visual details under complex prompts.
fix: External wrapper only: agentic prompt enhancement before generation plus VLM-located, segment-level visual semantic repair (edit selected frames into explicit references, then video-edit) after generation.
value: Commercial closed-source video models as of Aug 2026 still exhibit identity drift, incomplete instruction following and missing visual details under complex prompts, despite strong visual quality and motion realism — and cannot be fixed by parameter optimization.

evidence: Video generation models produce visually compelling results but systematically violate physical commonsense -- on VideoPhy-2, the best model achieves only 32.6% joint accuracy.
fix: NEWTON: an agentic planner builds physics-aware conditioning (keyframes, scientific computation, prompt refinement) with a verifier loop, lifting LTX-Video 21.4%->29.7% and Veo-3.1 30.7%->37.4% without touching the generator.
value: On VideoPhy-2 the best video model reaches only 32.6% joint accuracy (semantic adherence + physical commonsense); LTX-Video 21.4%, Veo-3.1 30.7%

evidence: We identify a specification bottleneck: text prompts are lossy compression of the physical world, omitting the parameters that fully determine dynamics, and no amount of model scaling can recover what was never specified.
fix: Condition on explicit physics (sufficiency, dynamism, verifiability) rather than richer prose.
value: Physics failures are a specification bottleneck, not a scale bottleneck: the text prompt omits the parameters that determine dynamics, so more model scale cannot recover them

evidence: Left free, the two generated characters drift to 21.2 m apart (recorded sessions stay near 5 m) and a third of frames show ground penetration. Two rules imposed on the explicit state, a terrain collider and a separation cap, cut penetration by 66% and keep the pair engaged, with no change to the observation model. Routing appearance through the predicted state costs no fidelity we can detect, at an FVD of 831 against 799 for recorded pose.
fix: Model an explicit world state and enforce constraints there (terrain collider, separation cap) — the appearance model needs no change.
value: FVD stayed flat (831 generated vs 799 recorded) on rollouts where two characters drifted 21.2 m apart against ~5 m in real sessions and a third of frames showed ground penetration

evidence: Reference-based metrics such as Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) and Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR) reward pixel fidelity over semantic correctness, while Frechet Video Distance (FVD) favors distributional textures over physical plausibility. Binary Visual Question Answering (VQA) based benchmarks like VBench~2.0 are prone to yes-bias and rely on low-resolution auditors that miss temporal failures.
fix: Replace binary VQA with Likert questionnaires graded by a VLM fed frames at native video resolution; note the human ceiling is not high either — inter-annotator agreement was 66.9% over 2,696 pairwise annotations.
value: The two dominant families of video scores are each blind in a stated way: SSIM/PSNR reward pixels over semantics, FVD rewards texture over physics, and binary-VQA benchmarks like VBench 2.0 carry yes-bias plus low-resolution auditors that miss temporal failures

evidence: Existing evaluation methods fail to accurately characterize these inconsistencies: fidelity-centric metrics like FVD are insensitive to geometric distortions, while consistency-focused benchmarks often penalize valid foreground dynamics.
fix: SGC: separate static from dynamic regions, estimate a local camera pose per background sub-region, and score the divergence among those poses.
value: FVD is insensitive to 3D geometric distortion, and consistency-focused benchmarks mis-penalise legitimate foreground motion

evidence: Applied to two driving WMs, the lower rungs reveal a reversal: the model that ranks higher on visual generation quality (L0) ranks lower on action-following (L1-L2), so visual fidelity does not predict the action-robustness a closed-loop verdict depends on.
fix: Accredit a generative world model on an admissibility ladder (L0-L4) before accepting its verdicts as evidence.
value: Visual-fidelity rank and action-following rank invert: the world model that scored higher on generation quality ranked lower on whether the world responds correctly to the policy's actions

evidence: Our resulting benchmark, Physics-IQ Verified, refines 57.6\% of all samples and improves over 34.8\% of prompts. In a comparison study using six image-to-video generative models, we observe moderate but meaningful ranking changes (Kendall's $\tau= 0.46$).
fix: Use Physics-IQ Verified (github.com/google-deepmind/physics-iq-benchmark) with its sample-level equal-weight scoring rather than the original.
value: Physics-IQ itself needed repair: an audit refined 57.6% of samples and improved 34.8% of prompts, and the corrected benchmark reorders six image-to-video models (Kendall's tau = 0.46 against the original ranking)

evidence: The strongest closed-source system we evaluate reaches 0.855 with a 33~pp performance gap across 11 systems, demonstrating substantial discriminative power. Moreover, high public-arena rankings fail to predict faithfulness, confirming that holistic Bradley-Terry (BT) preference scores prioritize aesthetics over fine-grained prompt adherence.
fix: Decompose a prompt into a DAG of yes/no constraints and zero out descendants of failed parents, so per-constraint failures are visible instead of averaged away.
value: Holistic arena preference (Bradley-Terry) does not predict prompt faithfulness; on a 310-prompt stress set with ~30 decomposed yes/no constraints each, the strongest closed-source system reaches 0.855 and the 11-system spread is 33 percentage points

evidence: For video generation, standard preference rewards can favor visually clean but nearly static outputs; introducing a new dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improve motions while improving overall VBench performance.
fix: Add an explicit dynamic-tracking reward alongside the preference reward.
value: Standard preference reward models used to tune video generators reward near-static output: visually clean, barely-moving videos win

evidence: Experiments on 19 leading MLLMs reveal substantial limitations in artifact perception and reasoning, with many models approaching random or even below-random performance in challenging settings. We further observe significant misalignment between MLLM judgments and human perceptual preferences, highlighting their limited reliability as general evaluators for AI-generated video realism.
value: MLLMs used as automatic realism judges are unreliable: across 19 leading MLLMs, many approach random or below-random performance on artifact identification and misalign with human perceptual preference

evidence: The refined taxonomy outperforms the global-schema baseline on held-out videos for every VLM tested, with a mean relative improvement of approximately 32%. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the per-VLM profiles expose model-specific blind spots that overall rankings cannot anticipate, with reliability patterns differing markedly across model families.
fix: JudgeFit: derive the evaluation taxonomy per judge model by calibrating its per-dimension scores against human physical-commonsense ratings.
value: A single global physics-evaluation schema mis-fits every VLM judge; per-VLM taxonomies beat the global schema on held-out video for all 16 VLMs tested, mean relative improvement ~32%, and expose model-specific blind spots invisible in aggregate rankings

evidence: However, errors introduced during self-rollout accumulate over long horizons, manifesting as color drift, motion stagnation, and eventual visual collapse.
fix: FreqForcing (training-free): anchor low-frequency components of anchor attention while keeping high-frequency local attention; extends a 5s-clip Self-Forcing model to two minutes (24x extrapolation).
value: Autoregressive long-video rollout degrades as low-frequency spectral energy drift, surfacing as color drift, motion stagnation and eventual visual collapse; attention sink only partially mitigates it

evidence: In particular, for 240s generation, it substantially improves overall and semantic scores while reducing quality drift from 7.84 to 1.33, demonstrating its effectiveness for stable long-horizon autoregressive video diffusion.
fix: TetherCache: split the KV cache into sink/memory/recent, select memory frames by attention relevance plus temporal diversity, and re-align recalled tokens' statistics to a trusted context distribution.
value: Quality drift on VBench-Long at 240 s generation measured 7.84 for the Self-Forcing baseline, reduced to 1.33 with cache management — drift grows across 30s/60s/240s settings

evidence: Furthermore, we find that pure training data scaling fails to boost model resistance to error drift, contradicting mainstream scaling paradigms.
fix: Video representation regularization; erank of hidden states works as a quantitative early indicator of drift (VBench Aesthetic 38.65->55.56, Imaging 44.37->72.08 vs Diffusion Forcing).
value: Scaling training data does NOT buy resistance to autoregressive drift; drift onset coincides with a sharp drop in the effective rank of hidden representations

evidence: This creates an irreversible generation trajectory: once the active window accumulates appearance errors, subsequent generations can only condition on this degraded trajectory and drift further away.
fix: Treat all previously generated latents as a searchable history and retrieve non-local context per block (LongLive-RAG).
value: Sliding-window autoregressive extension makes drift irreversible: once the active window holds appearance errors, later frames can only condition on the degraded trajectory

evidence: However, models are trained on clean ground-truth histories, while inference relies on their own generated histories, where accumulated errors cause identity drift, over-smoothing, and audio-visual desynchronization.
fix: Inject residual corruption at the matched flow-matching noise level it was produced at, rather than at an arbitrary level.
value: Training on clean ground-truth history but inferring on self-generated history produces identity drift, over-smoothing and audio-visual desynchronization in minute-scale audio-visual continuation

evidence: Even visually compelling videos frequently exhibit physical-state resets, abrupt affective shifts, and broken cinematic relations across shots.
fix: PersonaShot: ~1,000 multi-shot segments and 16 criterion-specific metrics scored by evaluators aligned to expert human judgment.
value: Across cuts in multi-shot generation, characters show physical-state resets, abrupt affective shifts and broken cinematic relations even when each shot looks good — perceptual quality and cross-shot continuity are separate axes

evidence: Current text-to-video models can make individual frames look convincing while still getting simple interactions wrong: objects move before contact, an intended action is skipped, a placed object keeps drifting, or a support relation breaks.
fix: Gate the denoising update to where an interaction is forming (token-level event signal with hysteresis and an early-step schedule) instead of updating every latent region at every step.
value: Interaction-level physics fails behind convincing frames: objects move before contact, the requested action is skipped, a placed object keeps drifting, support relations break

evidence: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling content but routinely violate elementary physics when the subject involves fluids: liquid columns break apart in mid-air, container water levels fail to rise as liquid is poured in, and splashes disperse without regard to momentum or gravity. We attribute this gap to the fact that large-scale video-text corpora contain almost no explicit motion supervision, so models learn to imitate fluid appearance rather than dynamics.
fix: Add an optical-flow decoder branch supervised with end-point-error losses on 1,638 MPM-simulated plus 2,320 real pouring videos: +8.75 VideoPhy-2 physical-commonsense and +4.65 video-quality points at 1.3B and 14B scale.
value: Fluid dynamics is imitated as appearance, not motion: liquid columns break apart in mid-air, container levels fail to rise while pouring, splashes ignore momentum and gravity — because web video-text corpora carry almost no explicit motion supervision

evidence: Across three proprietary and four open-source models, we find that Seedance 2.0 performs best overall, but all models remain far from robust physical understanding. Performance drops sharply on event-driven and environment-driven transitions, and even strong proprietary systems collapse on Anti-AV-Physics prompts.
fix: AV-Phys Agent: a ReAct-style evaluator pairing an MLLM with deterministic acoustic measurement tools; its rankings track human ratings.
value: Joint audio-video generators produce plausible sound that violates the visible acoustics; performance drops sharply on event-driven and environment-driven transitions and even strong proprietary systems collapse on deliberately anti-physical prompts

evidence: Our evaluation reveals a pronounced gap between strong audio-visual aesthetics and weak semantic reliability, including persistent failures in text rendering, speech coherence, physical reasoning, and a universal breakdown in musical pitch control.
value: Text-to-audio-video systems pair strong aesthetics with weak semantic reliability: persistent failures in text rendering, speech coherence and physical reasoning, and a universal breakdown in musical pitch control across 11 real-world prompt categories

evidence: SpatialGenEval involves 1,230 long, information-dense prompts across 25 real-world scenes. Each prompt integrates 10 spatial sub-domains and corresponding 10 multi-choice question-answer pairs, ranging from object position and layout to occlusion and causality. Our extensive evaluation of 21 state-of-the-art models reveals that higher-order spatial reasoning remains a primary bottleneck.
fix: Fine-tuning on rewritten information-dense pairs gave +4.2%/+5.7%/+4.4% on SDXL, Uniworld-V1, OmniGen2.
value: Prompt adherence collapses on long, information-dense prompts: on 1,230 long prompts across 25 scenes with 10 spatial sub-domains each, higher-order spatial reasoning is the primary bottleneck for 21 state-of-the-art T2I models

evidence: We conduct large-scale benchmarking on 26 popular image generation systems, including state-of-the-art commercial APIs and leading open-source models. The results reveal substantial capability gaps between current generative models and the requirements of professional visual content creation.
value: Structured design output (slides, charts, webpages, posters, scientific figures) exposes gaps closed by no current system: across 26 image-generation systems and 8,000 human-verified checklist questions, text rendering, layout control, attribute binding and knowledge reasoning all fall short of professional requirements

evidence: Despite their impressive performance, generative image models trained on large-scale datasets frequently fail to produce images with seemingly simple concepts -- e.g., human hands or objects appearing in groups of four -- that are reasonably expected to appear in the training data. These failure modes have largely been documented anecdotally, leaving open the question of whether they reflect idiosyncratic anomalies or more structural limitations of these models.
value: Conceptual blind spots are structural, not anecdotal: concepts well-represented in training data (human hands, objects in groups of four) are absent or misrepresented in generations, measured with a 32,000-concept sparse autoencoder over SD1.5/2.1, PixArt and Kandinsky

evidence: However, this mechanism can introduce lip leakage, where generated lips are influenced by the reference image rather than solely by the driving audio. Such leakage is difficult to detect with standard metrics and conventional test setup.
fix: Three-setup protocol — silent-input generation, mismatched audio-video pairing, matched synthesis — plus lip-sync discrepancy and silent-audio lip-sync scores.
value: Lip leakage in talking-face editing — lips driven by the identity reference image rather than by the audio — is not detectable with standard lip-sync metrics or conventional test setups

evidence: In recent years, Multi-Talker Audio-Video Generation (MTAVG) models have shown promising performance on fundamental metrics such as lip-sync and audio-visual alignment. However, these metrics remain insufficient for assessing cinematic expressiveness in scene-level generation.
value: Lip-sync and audio-visual alignment scores do not capture scene-level cinematic failure; a 10,000+ instance taxonomy of acting, narrative, atmosphere and audio-visual-language failures defeats even the strongest omni evaluators

evidence: What voice cloning does not do is reproduce the exact acoustics of the original recording. The output passes through the synthesis model, which has its own characteristics. A clone sounds like the speaker, but through the lens of the model's voice codec.
value: A voice clone is a model-mediated representation, never the original acoustics — the output always passes through the synthesis model's codec

evidence: There are inherent limitations: verification cannot guarantee that the provided recording truly belongs to the requester, only that the requester was present and actively participating.
value: Voice-clone verification proves presence, not ownership: it cannot establish that the supplied recording is the requester's own voice
