evidence: Unexpectedly, the audio-conditioned LDMs tends to predict lip movements based on visual information around the lips, such as facial muscles, eyes, and cheeks, while ignoring the audio information.
fix: Add SyncNet supervision and a fixed full-face mask not drawn from landmarks: 'without SyncNet supervision, as the mask size increases ... forcing the model to rely more on audio information, thereby improving lip-sync accuracy, and vice versa. In contrast, with SyncNet supervision, the model remains focused on learning audio-visual correlations across different mask sizes.'
value: Shortcut learning: audio-conditioned inpainting lipsync models predict lip motion from surrounding visual cues (cheeks, eyes, muscles) and ignore the audio — so a model can look plausible while barely listening

evidence: We observe that this broad evaluation criterion often favors a characteristic “AI aesthetic” meaning over-saturated colors, excessive focus on central subjects, pronounced bokeh effects, and convergence toward homogeneous styles. We term this phenomenon bakeyness .
fix: Decompose the eval: "we decompose T2I evaluation into five distinct dimensions: prompt following, aesthetic ... realism ... typography accuracy, and inference speed."
value: Single-axis "which image do you prefer?" preference evals reward a specific degenerate look — oversaturation, centred subject, heavy bokeh, style convergence — so a model can win preference benchmarks while getting less usable for real creative direction. BFL names the phenomenon bakeyness.

fix: If you need variation across seeds for the same prompt, do not pick by overall score; check the diversity dimension separately.
value: Diversity moves opposite to quality across the OneIG board: SD 1.5 scores 0.429 diversity while the modern leaders sit at 0.197 (Qwen-Image) and 0.151 (GPT Image 1). Headline overall scores hide that newer models mode-collapse across seeds.

evidence: Additionally, we notice occasional zoom-in and zoom-out effects across different models during editing.
fix: Compare input/output framing before accepting an edit; do not assume geometry is preserved.
value: Class-wide editing artifact: instruction-edit models silently rescale the frame, so a nominally local edit returns a differently-cropped image. Fatal for any pipeline that composites edited frames back into a fixed layout.

evidence: We have noticed a trade-off in video generation models between 1) temporal consistency ( Subject Consistency , Background Consistency , Temporal Flickering , Motion Smoothness ) and 2) Dynamic Degree . Models strong in temporal consistency often have a lower Dynamic Degree , as these two aspects are somewhat complementary (see Figure 2 and Table 1 ). For example, LaVie excels in Background Consistency and Temporal Flickering but has a low Dynamic Degree , probably because generating relatively static scenes can "cheat" to get high temporal consistency scores.
fix: Always pair a consistency score with the same model's Dynamic Degree; a high consistency score at low Dynamic Degree is a static-video artifact, not stability.
value: The four temporal dimensions (Subject Consistency, Background Consistency, Temporal Flickering, Motion Smoothness) can be gamed by generating near-static video; they trade off against Dynamic Degree and must never be read alone.

evidence: To evaluate subject consistency, we employ DINO [ 10 ] to extract features from each frame to represent the subject. Since DINO is not trained to disregard the differences within subjects of the same class [ 85 ] , its feature extraction is particularly sensitive to the identity variations of the subject within the video, thereby making it a suitable tool for evaluating subject consistency.
fix: For face identity use VBench-2.0's Human Identity dimension (ArcFace + RetinaFace), not Subject Consistency.
value: Subject Consistency is DINO frame-feature cosine similarity, i.e. appearance drift, not face identity; it is computed as similarity to the first frame and to the preceding frame, averaged.

evidence: To disentangle the evaluation of temporal flickering from other aspects, we use static video scenes ( i.e . , no apparent motions) as the test cases (We use carefully designed prompts to generate static scenes for video sampling. To further ensure that the evaluation is conducted on static videos without apparent motions, we employ an optical flow estimator [ 93 ] to filter out videos and only keep the static videos).
fix: The authors defend transfer via a human study across three dynamic levels with ~99% mutual correlation of rankings, but the number itself remains a static-scene measurement.
value: Temporal Flickering is measured ONLY on prompt-engineered static scenes, optical-flow-filtered to remove any with apparent motion — it does not measure flicker during motion.

evidence: where N is the number of videos generated by a model, T is the number of frames per video, f i t is the frame t in video i , and MAE is the Mean Absolute Error between two consecutive frames over all pixel locations.
value: Temporal Flickering is a raw pixel MAE between consecutive frames, normalized as (255 - MAE)/255 — any global brightness or camera drift scores as flicker, and sub-pixel identity wobble does not.

evidence: Specifically, video frame interpolation models usually assume real-world motions within a very short time period ( i.e . , a few consecutive frames) to be linear or quadratic and synthesize the non-existing intermediate frames based on this assumption.
fix: Interpret a high Motion Smoothness as "motion is locally predictable", which slow or low-amplitude motion also satisfies.
value: Motion Smoothness is not a physics measure: it drops the odd frames, re-interpolates them with AMT, and reports MAE against the originals — it rewards motion that a linear/quadratic interpolator can predict.

evidence: we uniformly sample 16 frames from each video and apply UMT [ 65 ] , which achieves the state-of-the-art classification performance on the Kinetics-400 dataset among open-sourced models to classify the action. The top 5 results with logits bigger than 0.85 are preserved as ground-truth candidates, and we check whether the actions mentioned in the text prompt appear in the ground-truth candidates.
value: Human Action is a UMT Kinetics-400 top-5 classification check with logit>0.85 over 16 sampled frames against 100 selected actions — a coarse pass/fail on action category, blind to execution quality, timing or mouth/face motion.

fix: Do not rank models for human-centric work on Human Action; use VBench-2.0 Human Anatomy / Human Identity / Motion Rationality instead.
value: Human Action is near-saturated and therefore non-discriminative: LaVie 96.80%, Gen-3 96.40%, CogVideoX-2B 98.00%, VideoCrafter-2.0 95.00%, Kling 93.40%, Gen-2 89.20%, Pika-1.0 86.20%.

evidence: Most models perform poorly in capturing Dynamic Spatial Relationships and Dynamic Attributes . Even in relatively simple cases, where an entity's position, relationship, or attribute ( e.g . , color) is instructed to change, and models fail in about 80% of the time.
fix: likely due to inadequate captioning granularity in video generation datasets — do not prompt for mid-shot attribute or position changes; stage them as separate shots.
value: Models fail roughly 80% of the time on simple instructed dynamic changes (an entity's position, relationship or attribute changing over the shot): Dynamic Attribute scores 22.71 / 24.18 / 8.06 / 19.41%, Dynamic Spatial Relationship 21.26 / 19.32 / 19.81 / 20.77% for HunyuanVideo / CogVideoX-1.5 / Sora / Kling 1.6.

evidence: A major limitation is that current foundation video generative models typically produce single-shot videos under 10 seconds in length, insufficient for conveying coherent narratives.
value: Complex Plot scores 10-12% across all four SOTA models because foundation T2V models emit single-shot clips under 10 seconds.

fix: Weight Color and Object Class deltas lightly; they are the least human-aligned dimensions in Table A5.
value: Human-alignment correlation is not uniform across dimensions: Motion Smoothness 99.80%, Subject Consistency 96.51%, Background Consistency 94.80%, Temporal Flickering 88.73%, Human Action 89.15%, but Color only 60.73%, Object Class 80.37%, Dynamic Degree 82.09%.

evidence: As video generative models continue to evolve, recent state-of-the-art models, including Sora [ 53 ] , Kling [ 69 ] , Gen-3 [ 59 ] , HunyuanVideo [ 72 ] , and Veo 2 [ 68 ] , have demonstrated strong performance on these metrics, and many aspects of superficial faithfulness are now approaching saturation.
value: The classic VBench dimensions are declared saturated by their own authors — they measure 'superficial faithfulness' (visual plausibility) rather than whether the video obeys real-world principles.

evidence: On the other hand, for categories involving complex and intense motions like Human and Vehicle (see their Dynamic Degree in Supplementary File), performance is relatively poor across all dimensions .
fix: A potential approach could involve integrating human-related priors or controls, such as skeletons, to better capture the articulated nature of human appearances and movements.
value: Human and Vehicle content — the categories with the most intense motion — score worst across ALL dimensions, spatial and temporal alike, and extra Human training data does not fix it (WebVid-10M is 26% Human, the largest share, yet Human is among the poorest categories).

evidence: Despite the significant progress that has been made in video generative models, existing state-of-the-art methods can only produce videos lasting 5-16 seconds, often labeled "long-form videos". Furthermore, videos exceeding 16 seconds struggle to maintain consistent character appearances and scene layouts throughout the narrative.
fix: Survey of 32 papers; the architectural components that consistently yield consistency are tabulated in the paper's taxonomy.
value: Published SOTA video generators top out at 5-16 seconds; past 16 seconds character appearance and scene layout stop holding. Methods that do reach ~150s trade it for frame redundancy and low temporal diversity.

evidence: Existing benchmarks primarily focus on 5--10 second text-conditioned generation and rarely support unified evaluation across text, image, and video conditioning modalities. Moreover, they provide limited insight into how identity consistency, narrative coherence, and audio-visual alignment degrade over extended temporal horizons.
fix: LongAV-Compass: 284 test cases across T2AV/I2AV/V2AV, 20+ dimensions incl. cross-segment consistency, scored with DINO-v2, ArcFace, CLIP, ImageBind; 11 models evaluated.
value: Identity-consistency benchmarks are built on 5-10 second clips and therefore cannot say how identity degrades over minute-scale horizons — the exact regime buyers care about.

evidence: Experiments on 17 representative LVG models reveal pronounced capability disparities across evaluation dimensions, with strong perceptual quality and background consistency but markedly weaker fine-grained text-video alignment and character consistency.
fix: LoCoT2V-Bench / LoCoT2V-Eval, released at github.com/XqZeppelinhead0702/LoCoT2V-Bench, adds temporal character consistency as an explicit dimension.
value: Across 17 long-video generation models, perceptual quality and background consistency are strong while fine-grained text alignment and CHARACTER consistency are markedly weak — the gap is systematic, not model-specific.

evidence: specifically, we observe that removing the visual anchoring mechanism results in a catastrophic drop in character consistency scores (from 7.99 to 0.55), confirming that visual priors are essential for identity preservation.
fix: Generate a per-character reference image with a T2I model first, then use it as the anchor for each scene's video generation.
value: Removing the image anchor (generating scenes from text alone instead of from a per-character reference image) collapses character consistency from 7.99 to 0.55 — a ~14x drop. Visual anchoring is not an improvement, it is the load-bearing mechanism.

evidence: The widely adopted chunk-wise paradigm introduces two fundamental failures: (1) temporal-spatial misalignment between static identity references and dynamic audio streams, and (2) cascading identity drift propagated through self-generated continuity references across chunks.
fix: AsymTalker: teacher anchored on ground-truth continuity references for drift-free supervision, student trained only on self-generated references; claims identity-consistent synthesis over 600-second videos at 66 FPS.
value: In chunk-wise long-form generation identity drift is CASCADING, not additive: each chunk is conditioned on the previous chunk's own generated continuity reference, so error is fed back into the conditioning signal.

evidence: Since current diffusion backbones lack any audio-related priors, this approach causes severe latent distribution error accumulation across video clips, leading the latent distribution of subsequent segments to drift away from the optimal distribution gradually.
fix: StableAvatar: Time-step-aware Audio Adapter (modulation instead of raw cross-attention injection), Audio Native Guidance at inference, dynamic weighted sliding-window latent fusion.
value: In audio-driven avatar video, long-form drift traces to audio modeling: off-the-shelf audio embeddings cross-attended into a backbone with no audio prior cause the LATENT DISTRIBUTION of each successive clip to drift away from the optimal one.

evidence: However, prior work exhibits limited efficiency in generating long-duration high-resolution videos, suffering from temporal drifting, quality degradation, and weak prompt following as video length increases.
fix: Spatio-temporal cascade: generate low-res blueprint keyframes capturing global semantics/motion first, then refine into high-res sub-clips with a first-last frame strategy.
value: Avatar models lose temporal stability, image quality AND prompt adherence together as requested video length grows — the three fail as one bundle, so a long clip is not just a drifting version of a short one.

evidence: Extensive experiments demonstrate that while current baselines struggle with continuous narrative logic or degenerate into trivial 2D sticker generators, our MuSS-augmented model achieves state-of-the-art narrative effectiveness and cross-shot identity preservation.
fix: MuSS proposes the Anti-Copy-Paste Variance (ACP-Var) metric plus a cross-shot matching mechanism in the training data to remove the shortcut; dataset sourced from 3,000+ movies.
value: Standard identity-similarity scoring rewards the copy-paste shortcut: a model that pastes the reference subject as a rigid 2D sticker scores well on identity while failing narrative and 3D structural consistency.

evidence: However, simply introducing additional reference images exacerbates the \textit{copy-paste} problem, particularly the \textbf{\textit{view-dependent copy-paste}} artifact, which reduces facial motion naturalness.
fix: Mv2ID: region-masking training to block shortcut learning, plus reference decoupled-RoPE giving video and conditioning tokens distinct positional encodings.
value: Adding MORE reference images to fix identity under large head-angle change makes things worse: it triggers a view-dependent copy-paste artifact that kills facial motion naturalness. Identity and naturalness trade against each other.

evidence: Prior methods often suffer from face-centric behavior that neglects body-level consistency, or produce copy-paste artifacts where subjects appear rigid due to pose locking.
fix: WildActor: Asymmetric Identity-Preserving Attention plus Viewpoint-Adaptive Monte Carlo Sampling that re-weights reference conditions by marginal utility; trained on Actor-18M (1.6M videos / 18M images).
value: Two opposite failure poles in identity-preserving human video: face-centric drift (body identity ignored) and pose locking (subject rigid, copy-paste). Optimizing away from one moves you toward the other.

evidence: Existing personalization methods often focus on facial identity but fail to preserve broader contextual cues such as hairstyle, outfit, and body shape, which are critical for visual coherence.
fix: ContextAnyone: jointly reconstruct the reference image while generating frames; Emphasize-Attention module and Gap-RoPE separating reference from video tokens.
value: Identity personalization that only targets the FACE still breaks visual coherence, because hairstyle, outfit and body shape drift independently of facial identity.

evidence: However, existing I2V models encounter difficulties in maintaining identity consistency between the input human image and the generated video, especially when the person in the video exhibits significant expression changes and movements. This issue becomes critical when the human face occupies merely a small fraction of the image.
fix: IPRO: RL tuning of the diffusion model against a face identity scorer, backpropagating reward through the last sampling steps, with a facial feature pool from ground-truth videos for multi-angle supervision and KL regularization. Demonstrated on Wan 2.2 I2V.
value: Identity consistency collapses specifically when the face occupies a small fraction of the frame, and when the subject shows large expression change or movement — not uniformly across all I2V content.

evidence: While advanced methods like VACE and Phantom have advanced video generation for specific subjects in diverse scenarios, they struggle with multi-human identity preservation in dynamic interactions, where consistent identities across multiple characters are critical.
fix: Identity-GRPO: video reward model trained on human-annotated + synthetic-distortion preference pairs, then a GRPO variant for multi-human consistency applied on top of VACE and Phantom.
value: Multi-human scenes are a distinct failure regime: VACE and Phantom hold single subjects but lose identity across multiple characters during dynamic interaction. Reported headroom is large — up to 18.9% gain on human-consistency metrics from RL alignment alone.

evidence: Streaming inference exacerbates these issues, leading to pronounced multimodal degradation, such as spatial blurring, temporal drift, and lip desynchronization, which creates an unresolved efficiency-performance trade-off.
fix: EchoTorrent: multi-teacher distillation, Adaptive CFG Calibration (ACC-DMD), Hybrid Long Tail Forcing aligning only tail frames during long-horizon self-rollout, and a pixel-domain VAE decoder refiner.
value: Streaming / real-time modes degrade differently from batch: spatial blurring, temporal drift AND lip desynchronization appear together, so a model's offline lipsync score does not transfer to its streaming mode.

evidence: Causal autoregressive video generation approaches enable efficient frame-by-frame generation but suffer from error accumulation, motion discontinuities at chunk boundaries, and degraded long-term consistency.
fix: Knot Forcing: cached KV of the reference image for global identity + sliding-window attention locally; a temporal knot module overlapping adjacent chunks; and a "running ahead" mechanism that advances the reference frame's temporal coordinate during inference.
value: Causal autoregressive portrait animation buys streaming latency at the cost of three named defects: error accumulation, visible motion discontinuity AT CHUNK BOUNDARIES, and degraded long-term consistency.

evidence: This static conditioning paradigm often creates a mismatch between fixed identity features and dynamically evolving facial motion, leading to identity drift, temporal inconsistency, and degraded perceptual quality.
fix: TT-SAC: parameter-free test-time loop that re-encodes the generator's own output to refine the conditioning representation — no retraining or gradients. Named baselines affected: AniTalker, FLOAT, Sonic.
value: Conditioning the whole clip on ONE static reference portrait is itself the drift mechanism: fixed identity features fall out of alignment with the evolving facial motion as the sequence proceeds.

evidence: However, end-to-end video generators are prone to appearance drift as motion accumulates and the depicted actions change.
fix: Training-free three-stage pipeline: rewrite each action into a terminal-state image prompt, generate a keyframe chain each conditioned on both reference identity and its predecessor, then fill intermediate segments with multi-reference guidance and identity-driven noise searching. Ranked 3rd on IPVG26 Track 2.
value: Appearance drifts as a function of accumulated MOTION and of action changes, not merely of elapsed time — a timestamped multi-action script is a harder identity test than a single-prompt clip of the same length.

evidence: Most existing solutions either compress historical frames using predefined strategies or retrieve keyframes based on coarse implicit attention signals, both of which fail to handle evolving prompts with shifting entity references, leading to identity drift, character duplication, and attribute loss.
fix: IAMFlow: LLM assigns global IDs to entities per prompt, VLM asynchronously verifies attributes from rendered frames. Released NarraStream-Bench (324 multi-prompt scripts, six dimensions); IAMFlow beats strongest baseline by 2.56 points in the 60-second multi-prompt setting.
value: With evolving multi-prompt narratives the failure is threefold and specific: identity drift, CHARACTER DUPLICATION (same person appears twice), and attribute loss — caused by memory schemes that compress history or retrieve keyframes by coarse attention.

evidence: This organization frequently leads to identity drift and semantic inconsistency when entities exit the frame or during interactive prompt transitions.
fix: SlotMemory: object-centric KV memory addressing "what" rather than "when". On 60-second interactive narratives with Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B it reports quality score 81.61 and +22.8% relative dynamic consistency over the strongest streaming baseline.
value: Identity drift is triggered by two concrete events rather than by duration alone: an entity LEAVING the frame and returning, and an interactive prompt transition.

evidence: Autoregressive diffusion enables real-time frame streaming, yet existing sliding-window caches discard past context, causing fidelity degradation, identity drift, and motion stagnation over long horizons.
fix: MemRoPE (training-free): memory tokens compressing all past keys into long-term and short-term EMA streams within a fixed cache, plus online RoPE indexing applying positional embeddings at attention time. Evaluated minute- to hour-scale.
value: Fixed-size sliding-window caches — the standard trick for unbounded generation — cause fidelity degradation, identity drift and motion stagnation because they discard past context; static attention-sink anchors do not fix it since the anchor cannot track evolving content.

evidence: Recent commercial video generation models have achieved strong visual quality and motion realism, but they still suffer from identity drift, incomplete instruction following, and missing visual details under complex prompts.
fix: AESR: agentic prompt enhancement learning model-specific prompting formats from official documentation and accumulating a reusable playbook, plus VLM-located segment repair that edits selected frames into explicit visual references for a video editing model. Ranked 1st, Track 1, ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge.
value: Closed-source commercial video models specifically fail on identity drift, incomplete instruction following and missing visual detail UNDER COMPLEX PROMPTS — and being black boxes, cannot be fixed by tuning.

evidence: As a result, structural failures in generated multi-talker dialogue videos, such as identity drift, unnatural turn transitions, and audio-visual misalignment, cannot be effectively diagnosed.
fix: MTAVG-Bench: 1.8k generated videos, 2.4k manually annotated QA pairs, hierarchical failure taxonomy across signal fidelity, temporal attribute consistency, social interaction and cinematic expression.
value: Multi-talker dialogue video has its own failure taxonomy — identity drift, unnatural turn transitions, audio-visual misalignment — which single-speaker benchmarks structurally cannot diagnose. Of 12 omni-models judged on detecting these, Gemini 3 Pro scored strongest overall.

evidence: Across seven text-to-video models, real reference footage advances ($ρ{=}{+}0.40$, $35\%$ static) while every generator shows near-zero progress and $92$--$100\%$ stasis; nine annotators rate real footage far above generated ($2.75$ vs.\ $0.99$ on a $0$--$4$ scale).
fix: Score 'progress' (directional attribute correlation) plus a stasis rate rather than local-reversal violation rates; enforce monotonicity by construction in a disentangled attribute latent.
value: Across 7 text-to-video models, irreversible physical processes (ice melting, paper charring) barely advance: 92-100% stasis rate vs 35% for real footage; human raters score real 2.75 vs generated 0.99 on a 0-4 scale. Generators do not reverse physics so much as fail to develop it.

evidence: Metrics of local reversal are null-degenerate: a per-clip violation rate scores $0.50$ on pure noise, and a variance-normalized reversal residual sits at its noise ceiling.
fix: Null-test every proposed physics metric on noise before reporting scores from it.
value: Physics-violation metrics of the 'local reversal' family are null-degenerate: a per-clip violation rate scores 0.50 on PURE NOISE, i.e. the metric cannot distinguish a generated video from static. Negative control was the thing that caught it.

evidence: For video generation, standard preference rewards can favor visually clean but nearly static outputs; introducing a new dynamic-tracking reward that substantially improve motions while improving overall VBench performance.
fix: Add an explicit dynamic-tracking reward alongside preference reward.
value: Standard human-preference reward models for video reward visually clean but nearly STATIC output — optimizing them suppresses motion. A dedicated dynamic-tracking reward was needed to recover motion while keeping VBench up.

evidence: Furthermore, its critic verifier mitigates the "cry-wolf" false-positive flaw of standard VLMs, lifting clean-clip accuracy from under 25% to over 80%.
fix: Route through dimension-specific specialists plus a critic-based verification stage rather than a monolithic VLM judge.
value: Off-the-shelf VLM judges 'cry wolf' on generated video: clean, defect-free clips are scored as defective, with clean-clip accuracy under 25% before a critic-verifier stage lifts it above 80%. A raw VLM-as-judge score is a false-positive machine.

evidence: We benchmark 16 frontier proprietary and open-source models and find that, while automatic perceptual-quality scores cluster tightly across systems, performance on Prompt Grounding and Scientific and Causal Correctness varies substantially, with a pronounced proprietary-open-source gap.
fix: Rubric-based protocol; the paper reports non-expert humans and MLLM judges reach high agreement with experts under it.
value: Perceptual-quality autoscores have saturated and no longer separate models: across 16 frontier proprietary and open T2V systems the perceptual scores cluster tightly while Prompt Grounding and causal correctness vary widely. Ranking by visual quality metrics ranks noise.

evidence: Recent methods often appear to deliver high safety with high utility, but this conclusion rests largely on coarse global utility metrics (e.g., FID, CLIPScore) that are insensitive to fine-grained semantic correctness, creating an illusion of high utility.
fix: Measure with TIFA-style structured question-answering; SAGE regularization restored +5.0% TIFA.
value: Coarse global metrics (FID, CLIPScore) are insensitive to fine-grained semantic correctness — object counts, attributes, relationships — producing an 'illusion of high utility'. Structured QA evaluation (TIFA) breaks the illusion.

evidence: Some methods leverage reinforcement learning to alleviate this issue, yet their reward models usually depend on text recognition systems that are insensitive to fine-grained glyph errors, so images with incorrect glyphs may still receive high rewards.
fix: Region-level glyph preference annotations with Region-Grouped DPO instead of an OCR reward model.
value: OCR-based text rewards used to train text rendering are insensitive to fine-grained glyph errors — an image with wrong glyphs can still collect a high reward. The reward model, not the generator, is the blind spot.

evidence: Critically, existing pure-vision encoders and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are strongly appearance-biased, lack temporal understanding, and thus struggle to discern intricate motion dynamics and anatomical implausibilities in generated videos.
fix: Metric built on a learned latent space of real human actions fusing appearance-agnostic skeletal geometry with appearance features; >68% improvement over prior SOTA on their benchmark.
value: Vision encoders and MLLMs used to score human motion in generated video are strongly APPEARANCE-biased and lack temporal understanding, so they miss motion-dynamics errors and anatomical implausibility (the hand/limb class of defect) entirely.

evidence: Optimizing models against these metrics encourages reward hacking, generating video-audio content that achieves high scores on these metrics yet appears incoherent or unfaithful to human viewers.
fix: Chain-of-thought omni-reward model trained on 10.3K fine-grained human paired comparisons (VAPref-10K).
value: Combining per-dimension audio/visual/sync metrics into a reward directly invites reward hacking: output scores high on every component metric while human viewers see it as incoherent and unfaithful.

evidence: Existing studies assess video quality through visual harmony, video-text consistency, and domain-specific alignment, yet lack quantitative metrics for measuring fidelity to physical laws.
fix: GeoCon-Bench: estimate global motion, fit homography/fundamental matrix on background correspondences, report inlier ratio and geometric error across frames.
value: No mainstream AIGC video-quality metric measures fidelity to physical law at all — visual harmony, video-text consistency and domain alignment are all the axes on offer.

evidence: However, errors introduced during self-rollout accumulate over long horizons, manifesting as color drift, motion stagnation, and eventual visual collapse.
fix: Spectral Self-Anchoring (training-free): anchor low-frequency components via anchor attention, keep motion from high-frequency local attention. Extends a 5s-trained Self-Forcing model to 2 minutes (24x extrapolation).
value: Autoregressive/streaming long-video rollout fails in a characteristic sequence: color drift, then motion stagnation, then visual collapse. Diagnosed in the frequency domain as low-frequency energy drift; attention sink alleviates but does not fix it.

evidence: Furthermore, we find that pure training data scaling fails to boost model resistance to error drift, contradicting mainstream scaling paradigms.
fix: Video representation regularization; vs Diffusion Forcing, VBench Aesthetic Quality 38.65 -> 55.56 and Imaging Quality 44.37 -> 72.08. erank proposed as the quantitative drift metric.
value: Compounding error in autoregressive video world models is coupled to DIMENSIONAL COLLAPSE of hidden representations — effective rank drops sharply at the onset of drift. Critically, scaling training data does NOT buy resistance to drift.

evidence: However, models are trained on clean ground-truth histories, while inference relies on their own generated histories, where accumulated errors cause identity drift, over-smoothing, and audio-visual desynchronization.
fix: Noise-level-aware residual correction (Vorch-Director, built on audio-visual LTX-2).
value: Train/inference history mismatch (clean ground-truth histories in training vs self-generated at inference) is the named cause of identity drift, over-smoothing, and audio-visual desync in minute-scale autoregressive continuation. Residual-correction fixes only work if the injected residual matches the flow-matching noise level it came from.

evidence: Second, the distillation-centric objective favours short-term generation but is prone to quality degradation when autoregressive errors accumulate over long rollouts.
fix: Train the two capabilities in parallel branches (full-parameter distillation + a long-horizon adapter via Recovery-oriented Rollout Training).
value: Few-step distillation and long-horizon robustness are in direct conflict: the distillation objective optimizes short-term quality and degrades as autoregressive error accumulates over long rollouts. Sequential distillation pipelines also propagate earlier-stage distribution shift into later stages.

evidence: However, most existing video diffusion models are trained with short videos, and degrade when extrapolated to long videos, struggling to maintain long-range temporal coherence while retaining diverse motions.
fix: Training-free Diff-VF: hybrid noise initialization, weighted window sampling, temporal extended sampling; evaluated on VBench-Long against FreeNoise, FreeLong, RIFLEx.
value: Video diffusion backbones are trained on short clips and degrade under extrapolation to long video, losing long-range temporal coherence when motion diversity is retained — the coherence/diversity trade is the failure axis, not raw frame quality.

evidence: Even visually compelling videos frequently exhibit physical-state resets, abrupt affective shifts, and broken cinematic relations across shots.
fix: PersonaShot: ~1,000 multi-shot segments, 16 metrics over physical continuity, affective dynamics, cinematic grammar, scored by criterion-specific evaluators.
value: Multi-shot narrative video: even visually compelling output shows physical-state RESETS across cuts, abrupt affective shifts, and broken cinematic relations. Perceptual quality and cross-shot continuity are measurably decoupled.

evidence: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling content but routinely violate elementary physics when the subject involves fluids: liquid columns break apart in mid-air, container water levels fail to rise as liquid is poured in, and splashes disperse without regard to momentum or gravity.
fix: Dual-stream optical-flow decoder branch with end-point-error supervision; +8.75 VideoPhy-2 Physical-Commonsense and +4.65 Video-Quality over frozen backbone, at 1.3B and 14B scales.
value: Fluid physics is a reliable break: liquid columns break apart mid-air, container water levels do not rise while pouring, splashes ignore momentum and gravity. Cause attributed to video-text corpora containing almost no explicit motion supervision — models imitate fluid APPEARANCE, not dynamics.

evidence: Failure analysis further shows that models rely on superficial visual patterns: image models fail to realize correct state changes, while video models further suffer from temporal inconsistencies.
fix: Test with unconventional and impossible tool/task pairings, not just regular ones.
value: World models generalize only over COMMON physical interactions. Tailor-Bench shows monotone degradation Regular -> Unconventional (substitute tool) -> Impossible (attribute-violating tool). Failure analysis: image models fail state changes, video models add temporal inconsistency on top.

evidence: VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks.
fix: Executable Blender code as a process-level chain of thought: simulate a deterministic draft, then draft-conditioned generative editing.
value: Physics headroom is large in absolute terms: the OmniWeaving baseline scores 0.475 on PhyGenBench and 52.18 on VBench-2.0; the best reported agentic pipeline reaches only 0.558 and 77.88. Physical consistency fails because temporal evolution must be inferred from a compressed text prompt.

evidence: State-of-the-art text-to-image (T2I) models exhibit pronounced and systematic defects when prompts involve intricate compositional factors such as multiple entities and multiple attributes.
fix: CO-AID dataset (defect locations + types) trains a model that both predicts defects and steers generation.
value: Human defect-spotting study over 651 compositional prompts across four categories — people, HAND, object, scene — with 29 participants labelling defect type and location per image. T2I defects are described as pronounced and SYSTEMATIC once prompts carry multiple entities and multiple attributes.

evidence: Experiments reveal that even leading generators still struggle with fundamental acoustic processes despite producing plausible sound events.
fix: AcoustiTrace: eight dimensions grounded in measurable acoustic quantities, with RGB-D acoustically annotated references.
value: Audio-video generators produce plausible, apparently synchronized sound that still violates the acoustics implied by the visible scene (source, propagation environment, reception). Plausibility of the sound EVENT is not evidence of correct acoustic process.

evidence: Results show that although current models achieve strong semantic adherence and visual quality, they often fail to faithfully capture fine-grained cultural details, particularly for underrepresented regions, rituals, and multimodal cultural cues.
fix: CultureVidBench, 1,000 prompts over 12 countries / 8 cultural regions / 14 cultural aspects.
value: Seven T2V models evaluated on 1,000 culture-specific prompts: strong semantic adherence and visual quality coexist with failure on fine-grained cultural detail, ritual procedure, and culturally appropriate visible text/audio — worst for underrepresented regions.

evidence: Our comprehensive experimental results reveal that most video generators achieve less than 20% of the compositional changes, highlighting enormous space for future improvement.
fix: Write prompts stating initial and final state explicitly; TC-Bench's transition-completeness metrics correlate with humans better than existing metrics.
value: Temporal compositionality (a prompt describing an initial state transitioning to a final state) is largely unrealized: most video generators complete under 20% of the described compositional changes. NOTE: TC-Bench is 2024-06, older than the 2025-2026 window, included because it is the sharpest single number on prompt adherence over time.

evidence: We find that existing automatic metrics (e.g., CLIPScore and FVD) correlate poorly with human evaluation.
fix: Fine-grained prompt categorization (content / controlled attribute / complexity, plus temporal categories) so metric reliability can be measured per scenario rather than in aggregate.
value: Foundational finding still cited as unresolved: CLIPScore and FVD correlate POORLY with human evaluation on T2V. NOTE: FETV is 2023-11, outside the requested window; reported because the 2026 papers above build on it rather than refute it.

evidence: Table 4: Failure mode analysis for models on SWE-BENCH PRO public set. We use LLM-as-a-judge to classify failing trajectories into buckets. Top LLMs, such as Opus 4.1 and GPT-5, are strong agents but struggle to produce solutions on high-complexity tasks. Weaker models, such as smaller open-source models, struggle with syntax, formatting, and tool-use.
value: SWE-Bench Pro failure buckets for agent trajectories, LLM-as-a-judge classified: Wrong solution, Tool-Use, Syntax error, Incorrect file, Endless File Reading, Misunderstood Problem Statement, Other. GPT-5 (high) failures are 72.8% wrong-solution; GPT-4o 27.9%, Qwen3 32B 52.7% — weaker models fail earlier in the pipeline, not later.

evidence: For example, SWE-bench Verified uses insufficient test cases, while TAU-bench counts empty responses as successful. Such issues can lead to under- or overestimation of agents' performance by up to 100% in relative terms.
fix: Apply the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC) before trusting an agentic score; on CVE-Bench it cut overestimation by 33%.
value: SWE-bench Verified itself is under-specified as a grader: insufficient test cases let wrong patches pass. Measured mis-estimation from such design faults reaches 100% in relative terms across agentic benchmarks.

evidence: We show that state-of-the-art models achieve up to 76% accuracy in identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions, without access to repository structure. This performance is merely up to 53% on tasks from repositories not included in SWE-Bench, pointing to possible data contamination or memorization.
value: A material share of SWE-bench Verified performance is memorization, not problem-solving: models locate the buggy file from the issue text alone at up to 76% on SWE-bench repos vs up to 53% on repos outside it (as of paper v4, 2025-12-01).

evidence: Providers like Google and OpenAI have received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all data on the arena, respectively. In contrast, a combined 83 open-weight models have only received an estimated 29.7% of the total data.
fix: Do not use Arena Elo as a general-quality proxy across vendors of unequal arena access; the paper's own framing is 'overfitting to Arena-specific dynamics rather than general model quality'.
value: LMArena / Chatbot Arena rankings are distorted by undisclosed private pre-release testing and unequal battle sampling: Google and OpenAI received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all arena data respectively, while 83 open-weight models combined got 29.7%. Extra arena data alone buys up to 112% relative gain on the arena distribution.

evidence: Across Chatbot Arena and six additional pairwise-comparison datasets, we show that modern leaderboards are non-robust across all three objectives: sub-1% targeted perturbations can change the top-ranked model, degrade Kendall's tau, and alter confidence intervals.
fix: Treat small Elo gaps between models as noise; require confidence intervals before acting on a rank change.
value: Bradley-Terry leaderboards including LMArena are not robust: targeted perturbation of under 1% of matches can change which model is ranked first (published 2026-05-15).

evidence: On three commonly used capability benchmarks: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), SimpleQA, and GPQA, we demonstrate that for approximately 3% of questions, search-based agents directly find the datasets with ground truth labels on HuggingFace.
fix: When quoting a search-agent benchmark score, state whether dataset-hosting domains were blocked during the run.
value: Search-enabled agents leak their own answers: on HLE, SimpleQA and GPQA about 3% of questions are answered by retrieving the labelled dataset from HuggingFace, and blocking HuggingFace drops accuracy on the contaminated subset by ~15%.

evidence: We show such benchmarks, and consequently multilingual evaluations, measure mathematical reasoning and factual recall, not multilingual proficiency. For example, thinking variants dramatically outperform instruct variants on these benchmarks, yet often perform worse on real-world multilingual tasks, such as LMArena.
fix: Evaluate multilingual generation with round-trip translation (Lost in Translation benchmark), which needs no reference translations or stronger judge.
value: Frontier multilingual eval numbers measure math and recall rather than multilingual proficiency; thinking variants beat instruct variants on them while doing worse on real multilingual use. Round-trip translation correlates rho=0.94 with LMArena user ratings (2026-04-14).

evidence: Furthermore, forensic examination of model divergence identified that half of the hardest GPQA items contain chemically or logically indefensible answers. The model's CoT revealed reasoning away from impossible answers, yielding penalization for accurate chemistry.
fix: Stop reading 1-2 point GPQA Diamond gaps between frontier models as capability differences; the label noise is larger.
value: GPQA Diamond has label validity problems at the hard end: forensic examination found half of the hardest items carry chemically or logically indefensible reference answers, and correct chemistry is scored as wrong (2026-03-04).

evidence: A particularly notable finding is that existing evaluation harnesses occasionally misjudge correct patches due to superficial discrepancies or hidden constraints.
value: The SWE-bench Verified harness itself produces false negatives: correct patches are graded as failures over superficial discrepancies or hidden constraints (2026-05-12 manual study of 900 trials).

evidence: An ablation study removing selected information types confirms that agents benefit less from information traditionally useful to humans, such as reproduction steps, and more from sentences that expose a repair direction, either through bug localization or a suggested fix.
fix: Rewrite bug-report templates for agents: lead with affected file/function/line and a proposed repair direction; drop long reproduction narratives.
value: Agent success on SWE-bench Verified is driven by what narrows the search space, not by what humans find useful: suggested fix in natural language OR 2.01, suggested fix in code OR 1.76, while references OR 0.80 and reproduction steps show no benefit; longer issues hurt (OR 0.73 per log-word).

evidence: Terminal-Bench 2.1. Kimi K3 is evaluated with the Kimi Code harness. For all other models, we report the best score across harnesses
fix: Never compare two models' agentic coding scores unless the harness, effort level and context strategy are identical; ask which harness produced each number.
value: Coding scores are harness-dependent by several points for the same weights: Kimi K3 scores 67.5 on DeepSWE with the Kimi Code harness but 67.3 with mini-SWE-agent, and 72.9 vs 73.7 on Kimi Code Bench 2.0 with Kimi Code vs Claude Code. The card reports 'best score across harnesses' for competitor models.

evidence: A brute-force Best-of-4 agent posts the higher raw factuality score (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) and would top a static leaderboard, but once cost is counted it is the worse system, losing on Q-Score (0.5169 vs 0.5217) at roughly four times the tokens and latency
fix: Compare candidate models on a cost-normalized metric (the paper's Q-Score protocol) rather than raw factuality when the raw scores are within a point of each other.
value: Static factuality leaderboards treat compute as free, so a brute-force Best-of-4 wrapper tops the board (H-Score 0.9169 vs 0.9103) while being the worse system once cost is counted (Q-Score 0.5169 vs 0.5217) at ~4x tokens and latency. Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-5 raw factuality is already bunched at the ceiling.

evidence: Table 3: Quantitative comparison on the CelebV dataset given different patch sizes of patch drop augmentation. A patch size of 0 indicates no patch drop.
value: Drift is measurable, not anecdotal. On 4-minute CelebV generations, removing patch-drop augmentation (patch size 0 = plain incremental generation) moves FID 38.518 -> 82.715 and FVD 491.338 -> 1088.158 while Sync-C barely moves (6.766 -> 6.683). Long-form failure shows up in image/video distance metrics, and sync scores stay silent about it.

evidence: As illustrated in Figure   6 , the extended inference duration significantly impacts FID metrics in existing diffusion-based approaches, leading to notable declines compared to their short-duration performance.
value: Benchmarks published on a few seconds of output do not transfer to minutes. Evaluated at 4 minutes, AniPortrait falls to Sync-C 3.810 / Sync-D 10.930 against real video 7.109 / 7.938, and Hallo to FID 82.715; parallel-generation methods (EchoMimic, AniPortrait) deteriorate most.
